summary: Turk_Yıldızları is a decision-focused health operating system for astronauts on long-duration missions such as lunar orbit. Instead of passive threshold alarms, it computes a personal-baseline resilience score per astronaut, explains each drop with numeric evidence, links it to a protocol with a responsible role and response target, projects time to threshold with uncertainty, and compares interventions by gain and operational cost. It uses NASA DONKI space weather and OSDR OSD-569 data. It is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device; biometrics are simulated.
details: Turk_Yıldızları is a decision-focused health operating system for astronauts on long-duration missions such as lunar orbit. Most existing tools only raise “threshold exceeded” alarms, yet with a 2.6-second communication delay and intermittent contact windows, a crew needs to know the cause, the action to take, and how much time remains. Our system answers five questions: the TY-RS v1 score evaluates six physiological subsystems against each astronaut’s own baseline; every drop is explained with numeric evidence and a confidence level; each alert is linked to one of six protocols with a responsible role and a response-time target; a 36-hour damped projection estimates time to threshold with an uncertainty band; and a counterfactual simulation ranks interventions by gain and operational cost. This aims to reduce alert fatigue, support timely and justified on-site decisions, and keep every action auditable after the mission, moving astronaut health monitoring from raising alarms to providing reasoned decision support. We built the system with Python and FastAPI (23 endpoints), MongoDB, and React 19, using NASA DONKI space weather data and NASA OSDR OSD-569 whole-blood RNA-seq data, and verified it with three independent suites totaling 129 automated checks. We used no dedicated hardware, and all biometric values are simulated. [We used AI-assisted coding; the scientific design, validation, and decisions were made by the team.] Our creativity lies in the counterfactual decision simulation, in making the system’s own uncertainty and limits part of every output, and in showing on screen the separation between what NASA measures and what we model; the molecular layer checks that our approach points in the same direction as real biology, but because the data are post-flight and n=4, it does not feed the score. In designing the system we considered operational reality, personal baselines, role-based privacy, three-layer resilience so that nothing degrades silently when NASA, the database, or the backend is unavailable, and accessibility. The system is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device: it does not diagnose, its weights are not clinically validated, and our next steps are to calibrate them with mission physicians and connect real sensors.
